proxy_language: Proto-Semitic (with Proto-Afroasiatic roots as deeper support); reconstructed notation following Kogan/Militarev-Kogan
proxy_rationale: Natufian (c. 14,500-11,500 BP, Levant) is known only archaeologically. Some scholars (Militarev, Blench, Bar-Yosef, Diakonoff-style Afroasiatic homeland arguments) link Natufians to early Afroasiatic/Proto-Semitic or Proto-Afroasiatic speakers, but this is contested (alternatives: pre-Semitic substrate, Proto-Afroasiatic with Cushitic/Chadic branches, or a lost language). Proto-Semitic roots with agricultural/pastoral and wild-resource vocabulary (wheat, gazelle, sickle, grind, stone, cave, tooth) are used as a defensible, openly speculative proxy; all forms are reconstructions and must be starred.
phonology: Proto-Semitic consonants (Huehnergard/Kogan): stops p b t d t' k g k' q? (emphatics glottalized: *t' *k' *s' etc., written with dot or apostrophe in scholarly notation as ṭ ḳ/q ṣ); fricatives *s *z *š *ś *ṣ *ṯ *ḏ *ṱ(ẓ) *ḫ *ġ *ḥ *ʕ *h; affricate-like *ś lateral; nasals *m *n; liquids *l *r; glides *w *y; glottal stop *ʔ. Vowels: *a *i *u with long counterparts *ā *ī *ū (no e/o). Three-vowel system; vowel length phonemic.
phonotactics: Syllable shapes CV, CVC, CVV(C); no initial vowel (words begin with a consonant, often glottal stop *ʔ-); no initial consonant clusters in reconstructed roots; medial clusters of CVC.CV type (e.g. *-rb-, *-ṭn-); final consonants allowed; word-final long vowels uncommon in roots (occur in suffixes). Roots are typically triconsonantal (C1-C2-C3) with some biconsonantal and quadriliteral roots. Stress not marked in reconstruction.
orthography: Standard Semitological transliteration in Latin script with starred reconstructions: ʔ ʕ ḥ ḫ ġ š ś ṣ ṭ ẓ ṯ ḏ q, macrons for long vowels (ā ī ū). For a game-safe Latin spelling, ASCII fallbacks may be used: ' for ʔ, ` or ' for ʕ, h/kh for ḥ/ḫ, sh for š, ts/s for ṣ, t for ṭ, q for q.
morphology: Root-and-pattern (templatic) morphology: triconsonantal root interdigitates with vowel patterns (e.g. qatl, qitl, qutl, qatal, qattāl 'agent/professional', maqtal 'place of', miqtal 'instrument'). Prefixes: ma- (place/instrument), ta- (abstract/instrument), ša- (causative), ʔa- (causative/elative). Suffixes: nominative -u, genitive -i, accusative -a (case in Proto-Semitic), mimation *-m (definite/indefinite state), feminine *-at, plural masculine *-ū/-ī, feminine plural *-āt, dual *-ā/-ayn. Reduplication marks intensives or plurals of small things. No definite article in Proto-Semitic proper.
compounding: Compounding is not native to Semitic; noun-noun relations are expressed by construct state/genitive: head noun (in bound/construct form, case-marked) followed by dependent noun in genitive. 'X of Y' = X-u Y-i (head first). 'Y-maker' or agent nouns use the qattāl pattern (e.g. *ṭabbāḫ-). Place names use ma- prefix (*ma-ʕrab 'place of setting' -> west). Names of gods/places can be construct chains: *bayt-u ʔil-i 'house of god' (cf. Beth-El).
noun_phrase_order: Head noun first; adjectives and genitives follow the noun and agree in gender/number/case (N-ADJ, N-GEN). Demonstratives and numerals may precede or follow (numerals 3-10 typically precede nouns in later Semitic). Possessive suffixes attach to head noun.

attested_roots.gloss: wheat, grain (cf. Akkadian kunāšu, Hebrew ḥiṭṭā)

sources: Huehnergard, John (2019) Proto-Semitic Language and Culture
Kogan, Leonid (2011) Proto-Semitic Phonology and Phonetics (in The Semitic Languages, ed. Weninger et al.)
Militarev, Alexander & Kogan, Leonid (2000-2005) Semitic Etymological Dictionary I-II

Blench, Roger (2006) Archaeology, Language and the African Past
notes: Entirely speculative proxy: the Natufian language is unknown and any Semitic/Afroasiatic link is contested; all roots are starred reconstructions from Proto-Semitic and should not be presented as attested Natufian. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word (language is not Goidelic). Avoid e and o vowels (absent in Proto-Semitic). Existing game names (Ghizagha, Cuc'ac, Hlathashi etc.) violate three-vowel and initial-glottal/consonant norms; rebuild with templatic roots and case endings.
